intro.title: Am I color blind?
intro.lead: Read the numbers hidden in {count} dot plates. It takes about 3 minutes and estimates red-green deficiency and its type.
intro.preview: This plate shows {n}. Can you see it? You get fresh plates in the test.
checklist: Turn off night mode, blue-light filters and True Tone
Use a moderately bright screen and look straight at it from about 50 cm
Wear your usual glasses or lenses
Answer within about 3 seconds. You cannot go back to previous plates
intro.note: Plates are redrawn and shuffled every time. The first plate is a demonstration that everyone can read.

test.instruction: Enter the number you see in the circle
test.hint: Keyboard: digits · Enter next · Backspace delete · N can't see

kinds.hidden: Hidden-digit plate · designed to appear only for {target} (reference)

verdictDesc.normal: You read most red-green plates. Your color vision looks within the normal range.
verdictDesc.protan: You mostly missed plates designed to vanish for protans (L-cone deficiency). Reds may look darker, and red, green and brown can be confused.
verdictDesc.deutan: You mostly missed plates designed to vanish for deutans (M-cone deficiency), the most common type. Green, orange and red can be confused.
verdictDesc.redGreen: You missed several red-green plates, but the type is unclear. It may be a mild deficiency or the effect of your screen.
verdictDesc.tritan: You read the red-green plates but not the blue-yellow ones. Tritan deficiency is very rare and depends heavily on how your screen shows blue, so turn off screen filters and try again.
verdictDesc.unclear: You missed the demonstration plate or most plates. Screen settings (night mode, filters, brightness) or attention are likely factors, so no verdict is given.

confidenceDesc.high: Your answers point consistently in one direction. Still, a screen test is less accurate than printed plates.
confidenceDesc.medium: Mostly consistent, with some borderline answers. Try again with different lighting or screen.
confidenceDesc.low: Your answers are mixed, so this result alone is not conclusive. Retake the test or see an eye doctor.

disclaimer.title: This is not a medical diagnosis
items: Results vary with screen color, brightness and room lighting
Night mode or blue-light filters can make people with normal vision fail
Get a proper diagnosis from an eye doctor (Ishihara plates, anomaloscope)

share.label: My color vision test result
share.text: Color vision test {correct}/{total} correct · {verdict}. Am I color blind? Find out in 3 minutes

colorBlindTest.title: Color Blind Test
colorBlindTest.description: A self-check with 14 Ishihara-style pseudo-isochromatic plates for red-green color vision deficiency.

result.simulatorDesc: See how photos and designs look to people with color vision deficiency in the simulator.
result.viewDesc: Use the buttons to compare how each plate looks to each type of color vision (dichromat simulation: Viénot 1999 for red-green; tritan uses the same projection with the Brettel 1997 660 nm anchor).
result.title: Test Results
result.moderate: Color deficiency possible. Eye exam recommended
result.disclaimer: This is a screening tool only. See an eye doctor for accurate diagnosis

about.title: About the Test
items: A screening test based on the Ishihara plate principle
Plate colors are computed on dichromat confusion lines and redrawn every time
1 demonstration, 5 vanishing, 2 transformation, 2 classification, 2 hidden-digit and 2 blue-yellow plates (14 total)
Use a bright room, turn off screen filters and look straight at the screen

types.title: Types of Color Deficiency
items: Total color blindness: Cannot distinguish colors (very rare)
Congenital color vision deficiency affects about 8% of men of Northern European descent and 0.5% of women (Korea: about 5.9% of men, 0.4% of women)

whatIs.title: What is the Color Blind Test?
whatIs.description: The Color Blind Test is an online screening tool that follows the principle of the Ishihara color vision test plates. Users read numbers hidden within patterns of colored dots to detect possible red-green color blindness or color weakness. While not a substitute for a formal medical diagnosis, it provides a quick way to screen for potential color vision deficiency.

howToUse.title: How to Use
items: 1. Turn off night mode and blue-light filters and sit about 50 cm from the screen.
2. Enter the number you see with the number pad. If you see none, press 'Can't see'.
3. You can't go back, so answer with your first impression.
4. Check the verdict, confidence and how each plate looks to color-deficient viewers.

tips.title: Pro Tips
items: Set your monitor to a comfortable brightness level and avoid screen glare for accurate results.
Take the test with your usual glasses or contact lenses on.
If color vision deficiency is suspected, visit an ophthalmologist for a formal Ishihara or Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue test.

items.q: Can this test accurately diagnose color blindness?
items.a: No. This is a quick screening tool only. A formal diagnosis requires professional testing by an eye care specialist.

items.q: What is the difference between color blindness and color weakness?
items.a: Color blindness means a complete inability to distinguish certain colors, while color weakness (color deficiency) means reduced ability to differentiate colors. Color weakness is far more common. Congenital color vision deficiency of either kind affects about 8% of men of Northern European descent and 0.5% of women (in Korea about 5.9% of men and 0.4% of women).

items.q: Is there a treatment for color vision deficiency?
items.a: There is currently no cure for congenital color vision deficiency. However, special color correction glasses (e.g., EnChroma) may help some individuals with color weakness.
